issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: For a 35-year-old single male special education teacher reporting a mugging/robbery, 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile. The other appraisals center on self-blame and persistent danger, but this item implies a salient role failure theme (e.g. partner/parent/protector) that is not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, or memory.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense shame and intense rage on recall can coexist, but paired with a mugging/robbery and the rest of this profile they pull toward different meanings of the event without enough support elsewhere. Shame would usually connect to strong self-blame/humiliation themes, while rage would connect to injustice/anger themes; the profile does not integrate both clearly.

vignette: Liam had always been a laid-back person, but that all changed on the night he was mugged on his way home from work. It was a typical Wednesday evening when he walked out of the school building where he taught special education classes, lost in thought as he strolled through the dimly lit streets. Suddenly, a group of teenagers jumped him, knocking him to the ground and making off with his wallet and phone. The attack was over in seconds, but its impact would linger for months to come. As Liam struggled to process what had happened, certain sights and sounds began to trigger memories of that night. Shouting, whether it was a child misbehaving in class or someone yelling on the street, made him instantly tense up, transporting him back to the moment when his attackers were screaming at him to hand over his valuables. Even somatic pain like neck strain could bring it all flooding back, as if his body was recalling the physical sensations of being pinned to the ground. When Liam's mind began to wander, he would often find himself scanning for exits in any room or building he entered, a habit that made him feel safer but also contributed to his growing sense of unease. He became increasingly hypervigilant, always on the lookout for potential threats, convinced that if he let his guard down for even a moment, something terrible would happen. "I have to be on guard all the time," he told himself, "because if I'm not, I'll end up like that again." These negative appraisals - that he was inadequate and should have been able to prevent the attack - began to colour his memories of that night. When Liam recalled the event, it was with vivid photographic detail, as if looking at snapshots in his mind. But those images were also infused with intense rage and guilt, emotions that left him feeling like he'd failed somehow. "Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation," he berated himself. As time went on, these negative appraisals only deepened Liam's sense of threat. He became convinced that the world was a perilous place, full of lurking dangers waiting to pounce. This perception made him even more hypervigilant, constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of trouble - and finding them everywhere. Authority figures like police officers, who were supposed to be there to help, only triggered more anxiety in Liam, serving as reminders that he was vulnerable to attack at any moment. The cycle of threat and memory proved particularly debilitating for Liam. When he felt threatened, it brought the memories flooding back, which in turn reinforced his sense of danger - a self-reinforcing loop that left him feeling trapped and helpless. Even small things like a sudden noise or an unfamiliar face could set off this chain reaction, plunging Liam into a state of heightened anxiety. Liam's inability to relax, even in safe spaces, only added to his distress. He would try to calm himself down, but his mind would start racing with worst-case scenarios, making it impossible for him to unwind. "I am unable to relax," he confessed, "even when I know I'm in a safe place." The memories of that night continued to haunt him, surfacing at unexpected moments - like during a flashback, when Liam suddenly felt as if the attack was happening all over again. It wasn't until Liam's students began to notice his increasing irritability and withdrawal that he realized he needed help. They would ask him questions in class, only to be met with a brusque response or an uncharacteristic outburst of anger. His relationships with colleagues started to suffer as well, as Liam became more isolated and withdrawn. He knew he couldn't keep going on like this - something had to give. Liam's decision to seek help was motivated by a desire to break free from the cycle of threat and memory that had taken over his life. He hoped that therapy could help him learn to manage his anxiety, challenge his negative appraisals, and find ways to relax in a world that no longer felt safe. But as he sat in the therapist's office, waiting for their first session to begin, Liam couldn't shake off the feeling of vulnerability - the sense that he was still on edge, waiting for the next attack to come.
